catalog_quote: The sound system of Tamagário contains the following consonants and vowels: p [p, b], t [t, d, ts, s], k [k, g, kx, x, ɣ] (all these are backed when contiguous to a, o, or u); m [m, b], n [n, d]; w, y, r [ř, r̃]; i [i, ɩ], e [e, ɛ], a [a, æ, ɑ], o [o, ɔ], u [u, ʊ], and perhaps ə. The language is non-tonal; in bisyllabic words the final syllable is stressed.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (116 pp., ANU scan of Voorhoeve 1975, Pacific Linguistics C-38 pp. 345-460). PDF page 23 = printed p. 367, section 2.6.2.2.5.1 'Tamagário' inside 2.6.2.2.5 'The Kayagar Stock-level Family'. Rendered the page with page render and read the image: after the consonant/vowel inventory the sentence reads exactly 'The language is non-tonal; in bisyllabic words the final syllable is stressed.' — verbatim match. The text layer agrees (with scan spacing noise). Context: p. 366-367 introduces the Kayagar family in the Gondu and Cook river basins north-west of Yaqay, three languages Kaugat (~700), Kaygir (~3,000), Tamagario (~3,500), Tamagario in two dialects; sources = Voorhoeve's own 1970 fiel…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Tamagario has no tone; word stress falls on the final syllable, stated explicitly for bisyllabic words (no statement is made for longer words). Voorhoeve 1971: 85 adds that in word-final clusters /pm/ and /tn/ the syllabic nasal itself can carry the stress ([pm̩], [tn̩]), consistent with final stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None mentioned; the rule is stated only for bisyllabic words, so polysyllables are not covered.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level, from elicited wordlists (Voorhoeve's own 1970 fieldwork, one wordlist from a young man of Arare, Tamario dialect area, plus Drabbe's unpublished sketch). Only one sentence; no examples of stress placement are given in the source. The same one-line statement is made for the sister language Kaygir (p. 368).
new_statements.identity_note: Voorhoeve's Tamagario data come from one wordlist elicited from a young man of Arare (Tamario/central dialect area) plus Drabbe's unpublished sketch; the Yogo (Joggo) dialect is not separately described. The SIL 2010 survey villages (Kaitok, Sigare, Yame) belong to the Yogo dialect area per Voorhoeve 1975's checklist, and their speakers call the language Wiyagar. The stress statement therefore applies to Tamagario proper (tama1336, Tamario dialect); Voorhoeve makes the identical statement for the sister language Kaygir (kaya1327 / ISO kyt).

SAME WORK: file line 1 '====== Gondu River ======', line 3 'Timothy Usher, Santa Fe Institute'; Situation sentence names 'Yogo (Jogo, Joggo) Tamagario (Tamario, Tamaraw) and Kaigir (Kajgir, Kaygir, also known as Kayagar).. the Cook River family, also known as the Kayagar (Kajagar) family (Voorhoeve 1971: 79-82, 1975: 366-367.)' and the Historical phonology section gives the proto-Gondu River inventory with Voorhoeve's proto-Kajagar table = the cited 'Kayagar family page with proto-Kayagar recons…
new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog record (Voorhoeve 1975: 367 'in bisyllabic words the final syllable is stressed' -> fixed final) and adds: the domain (nominals), a diachronic account (loss of unstressed final vowels), stressable final syllabic nasals (from Voorhoeve 1971: 85, already noted held by the project as silent-on-placement), and a variety-level caveat that Yogo trends toward initial stress. Usher's statement is partly derivative of Voorhoeve plus SIL survey transcriptions (Lebold et al. 2010, Kriens et al. 2011), not new fieldwork.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Family-level statement for Gondu River (Yogo, Tamagario, Kaigir): stress generally falls on the final syllable of nominals, explained diachronically by the loss of unstressed final vowels in Cook and Gondu River; word-final syllabic nasals in /pm/, /tn/ clusters can bear the stress (after Voorhoeve 1971: 85). The cognate tables transcribe Tamagario (Arare, Kriens et al. 2011) forms with final stress in disyllables, e.g. baˈrap 'tongue', baˈpʰu 'child', kopˈrap 'white', orːˈpʰam 'rattan', ɣaˈpri 'eat'.
new_statements.exceptions: 'generally' (nominals only are named); 'In Yogo there has been a trend towards initial stress' - Yogo (Jogo/Joggo), which Voorhoeve and Glottolog count as a dialect of Tamagario but Usher treats as a separate Gondu River language (Yogo forms in the tables show mixed placement, e.g. ˈbopu 'child' vs kɔˈpːɾɔp 'white').
new_statements.identity_note: Usher's stress sentence is a family-level statement for 'Gondu River' (Yogo, Tamagario, Kaigir; = Voorhoeve's Kayagar family minus Atohwaim/Kaugat), in a historical-phonology section signed Timothy Usher, Santa Fe Institute, page rev. 2024-06-25; the Tamagario data behind it are Voorhoeve (1971, 1975; Arare village, Tamario dialect, after Drabbe's ms) and Kriens, Lebold & Menanti (2011; Arare, Pagai - villages that survey reassigns to Kayagar/Kaigir) plus Lebold et al. (2010) for Yogo (Kaitok, Sigare, Yame). The dedicated Tamagario page has no stress sentence. The catalog record rests on Voorhoeve 1975: 367 (Tamario/Arare).
